root_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every prime p > 3, define I: {1,...,p-1} -> {1,...,p-1} by I(k) being the unique integer with k * I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p). Let S = { k ∈ {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }. Then |S| > p/4 - 1. Equivalently (since |S| is integral), |S| ≥ floor(p/4).

Define S = { k in {1,...,p-2} : I(k+1) < I(k) }
Claim: |S| > p/4 - 1 (equivalently, |S| ≥ floor(p/4) since |S| is an integer)

payload.theorem_nl: Let $p$ be a prime number greater than $3$. For each $k \\in \\{1,\\dots,p-1\\}$, let $I(k) \\in \\{1,2,\\dots,p-1\\}$ be such that $k \\cdot I(k) \\equiv 1 \\pmod{p}$. Prove that the number of integers $k \\in \\{1,\\dots,p-2\\}$ such that $I(k+1) < I(k)$ is greater than $p/4-1$.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix a prime p>3 and define the inverse permutation I and the descent set S as in the theorem. Introduce the auxiliary integers a_k=(kI(k)-1)/p. First use the algebraic equivalence between descents of I and non-increases of the sequence a_k. Next isolate the explicit central descent at c=(p-1)/2. Then use the symmetry I(p-m)=p-I(m) to deduce that S is symmetric under reflection about c. Separately, prove on the first half of the sequence (a_1,...,a_c) that five consecutive strict increases are impossible; a correct block-counting lemma then yields at least floor((c-1)/4) non-increase positions in {1,...,c-1}, hence at least that many descents in the left half of S. By reflection the same number occurs in the right half. Adding the central descent gives |S| >= 2 floor((c-1)/4)+1, and an elementary floor inequality shows this is at least floor(p/4). Since |S| is the number counted in the theorem, this implies |S| > p/4 - 1 exactly as required.

steps.derives: For the fixed prime p>3, the integers a_k=(k*I(k)-1)/p are well-defined for 1<=k<=p-1, and for 2<=k<=p-1 they satisfy 1<=a_k<=k-1.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the content of L1 after instantiating the fixed prime p from the root theorem.

steps.derives: For every k in {1,...,p-2}, k belongs to S = { j in {1,...,p-2} : I(j+1)<I(j) } if and only if a_{k+1} <= a_k.
steps.trivial_justification: L2 directly identifies the descent predicate defining S with the non-increase predicate for the auxiliary sequence a_k.

steps.derives: If c=(p-1)/2, then c belongs to S.
steps.trivial_justification: L3 gives explicit values I(c)=p-2 and I(c+1)=2, so I(c+1)<I(c), hence c∈S.

steps.derives: The set S is symmetric under the reflection k ↦ p-k-1. In particular, the reflection maps S ∩ {1,...,c-1} bijectively onto S ∩ {c+1,...,p-2}, where c=(p-1)/2.
steps.trivial_justification: L4 gives the pointwise equivalence k∈S iff p-k-1∈S. For 1<=k<=c-1, the reflected index p-k-1 lies in {c+1,...,p-2}; conversely every index in {c+1,...,p-2} is the reflection of a unique index in {1,...,c-1}. Therefore reflection restricts to a bijection between the left and right portions of S.

steps.derives: The left-half subset S_left := S ∩ {1,...,c-1} satisfies |S_left| >= floor((c-1)/4), where c=(p-1)/2.
steps.trivial_justification: This is exactly the conclusion of L7 for the present prime p and the set S.

steps.derives: The right-half subset S_right := S ∩ {c+1,...,p-2} satisfies |S_right| = |S_left| >= floor((c-1)/4).
steps.trivial_justification: By A4, reflection gives a bijection S_left ≃ S_right, so the two sets have equal cardinality. Combining with the lower bound from A5 yields |S_right| >= floor((c-1)/4).

The sets S_left, {c}, and S_right are pairwise disjoint and their union is contained in S; indeed A3 gives c∈S, A5 bounds |S_left|, and A6 bounds |S_right|. Therefore |S| >= |S_left| + 1 + |S_right| >= 2*floor((c-1)/4)+1.
Apply L8 to c=(p-1)/2 to obtain 2*floor((c-1)/4)+1 >= floor(p/4). Combining this with A7 gives |S| >= floor(p/4).

steps.derives: The number of integers k in {1,...,p-2} such that I(k+1) < I(k) is greater than p/4 - 1.
steps.trivial_justification: By definition, |S| is exactly the number of integers k in {1,...,p-2} with I(k+1)<I(k). Since |S| is an integer and A8 gives |S| >= floor(p/4), it follows that |S| > p/4 - 1. This is equivalent to the root theorem statement.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Sets up the auxiliary arithmetic sequence a_k used to replace descents of I by order comparisons on smaller integers.
lemmas.self_check_notes: Integrality is immediate from k*I(k) ≡ 1 mod p. Bounds follow from 1<k*I(k)<k*p for k>=2. Coprimality follows from gcd(k, p*a_k+1)=1.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For prime p>3, if I(k) is the inverse of k modulo p in {1,...,p-1} and a_k=(k*I(k)-1)/p, then a_k is an integer for all k, and for 2<=k<=p-1 we have 1<=a_k<=k-1 and gcd(a_k,k)=1.

a_k depends on p and I(k), hence on p and k

lemmas.statement_nl: Let p be a prime number greater than 3. For each k in {1,...,p-1}, let I(k) in {1,...,p-1} satisfy k*I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p), and define a_k = (k*I(k)-1)/p. Then for every k in {1,...,p-1}, the number a_k is an integer, and for every k in {2,...,p-1} one has 1 <= a_k <= k-1. Moreover gcd(a_k,k)=1.

lemmas.role_in_assembly: Translates the theorem from descents of inverse values to a monotonicity statement about the quotient sequence a_k.
lemmas.self_check_notes: Substitute I(k)=(p*a_k+1)/k and I(k+1)=(p*a_{k+1}+1)/(k+1); after clearing denominators the strict inequality is equivalent to p(k*a_{k+1}-(k+1)a_k) < 1-a_k <= 0, hence to k*a_{k+1} <= (k+1)a_k, which is equivalent to a_{k+1}<=a_k.

semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For prime p>3 and 1<=k<=p-2, with a_k=(k*I(k)-1)/p and a_{k+1}=((k+1)*I(k+1)-1)/p, one has I(k+1)<I(k) iff a_{k+1}<=a_k.

Claim equivalence between descent and non-increase
witness_dependencies: I(k) and I(k+1) depend on p and k
a_k,a_{k+1} depend on p and the corresponding inverse values

lemmas.statement_nl: Let p be a prime number greater than 3. For each k in {1,...,p-1}, let I(k) in {1,...,p-1} satisfy k*I(k) ≡ 1 (mod p), and define a_k = (k*I(k)-1)/p. Then for every k in {1,...,p-2}, the inequality I(k+1) < I(k) holds if and only if a_{k+1} <= a_k.

candidates.strategy_summary: Use a genuinely different strategy from the rejected local-4-block attempts: instead of trying to deduce the theorem from a weak interval-hitting property of the descent set, rewrite the inverse values via the quotients a_k=(k I(k)-1)/p, convert descents of I into non-increases of the sequence a_k, and then use a stronger arithmetic counting statement on the a_k-sequence together with a separate central-index argument. This explicitly avoids the previously rejected false covering lemmas and the off-by-one interval-counting gap.
